parsed.explanation: Two regimes combine. The division is among the country's most protective: operative public-accommodation, employment and housing protections (ballot-retained 2018), gender-identity hate-crime coverage with a functioning reporting unit, self-ID documents including X markers, confidential name changes, and a 2022 shield law protecting a visitor's care even where their home jurisdiction bans it. No facility ban or bathroom criminalisation is documented here. But federal rules govern entry, federally funded facilities and custody, and cannot be preempted: the February 2025 cable directs refusal where documents cast doubt on sex (possible lifetime fraud finding), X markers are stopped, foreign governments issued travel advisories, and trans immigration detainees document beatings, solitary and sexual abuse by guards. Outing in daily life brings friction with recourse; outing at the border brings policy-directed exclusion and, if detained, documented custodial harm. Unresolved litigation keeps outcomes uncertain.

entry_documents.exposure: Federal February 2025 cable directs officers to refuse cases where document discrepancy casts reasonable doubt on sex, and to consider a permanent fraud ineligibility finding; X-marker passports discontinued; several foreign governments issued travel advisories for trans visitors.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X-marker passports remain valid to expiry; the fraud finding requires four elements, has limited waivers and is never automatic; the passport suit remains pending in national courts.
entry_documents.interaction: Division self-ID document practice cannot affect federal visa adjudication or border inspection; a state-issued matching ID does not cure federal sex scrutiny.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Documented pattern in federal immigration custody: transgender men subjected to identity-motivated forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse. From 2026 federal corrections adopt conversion-therapy-style policies (hair cutting, hormone removal).
investigation_detention_custody.protection: National hate-crimes statute; several executive orders blocked or enjoined; legal-aid FAQ on document rules; division courts and equality bodies function.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Document discrepancy can escalate to investigation, detention and birth-sex placement entirely under federal authority, outside division protection.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Federal order bars transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities nationwide, including federal buildings inside this division; 21+ divisions restrict facility use and 4 criminalise in some circumstances.
federal_state_facilities.protection: This division has no documented facility ban or criminal provision and is ranked 'Most Protective'; public accommodations must serve visitors without regard to gender identity since 2016.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Division protection covers hotels, shops, restaurants and transport but does not reach federally owned or federally funded settings.

care_services.exposure: Federal orders and October 2025 proposed rules restrict and defund gender-affirming care; DOJ subpoenaed under-19 patient records nationally.
care_services.protection: Division shield law (2022) protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where care lawful here was banned in the visitor's home jurisdiction; 2022 codified care protections; conversion therapy on minors banned.
care_services.interaction: Shield binds division providers; federally funded facilities may apply federal funding rules despite state law.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Federal counterterrorism strategy prioritises groups 'radically pro-transgender'; DOJ guidance uses 'radical gender ideology'; orders direct law enforcement into schools and rescind name/pronoun policies, creating official threat-framing.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Gender ideology is never a reward criterion; the strategy states counterterrorism will not target mere disagreement; several orders enjoined; division police operate under a gender-identity hate-crime statute.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Federal framing raises street-level hostility odds while division institutions remain protective, producing uneven exposure by setting.

minors_guardians.exposure: Federal order directs criminal investigation of those facilitating a trans minor's social transition; under-19 medical records subpoenaed; youth-care bans in 27 divisions and proposed federal insurance bar apply elsewhere in the country.
minors_guardians.protection: Division bans conversion therapy, funds anti-bullying reporting, and documents no youth-care ban; shield law covers a visiting minor's care sought here.
minors_guardians.interaction: A visiting family's care in this division is shielded at state level, but federally funded clinics and border encounters follow federal rules.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: National bias-crime reporting shows sustained anti-LGBTQ hostility; official rhetoric and pending bills may embolden confrontations; no division-specific pattern of trans killings is documented.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Division hate-crime statute covers gender identity since 2012 with a reporting unit, task force and mandatory public summaries; public accommodations retained by 67.8% vote; 2020 national employment ruling and federal hate-crime law apply.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Assault is prosecuted under state machinery that is documented as operating, cushioning national climate effects.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Passport suit, executive-order challenges and proposed health rules unresolved, so operative rules at travel time are uncertain; two unenforceable sodomy-era code provisions remain unrepealed after stalled repeal efforts.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Legal-aid FAQ tracks document rules; civil-liberties litigation active; division equality bodies, courts and shield listing (current to September 2026) are documented as functioning.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Division remedies cannot cure federal border refusal or federal custody conduct; national uncertainty persists despite strong local recourse.

anchor_checks.comparison: Vellandra imposes a categorical register barring every transgender visitor with no effective remedy, so exclusion is universal and complete. Here no categorical bar exists: refusal requires a document discrepancy or doubt about sex, waiver routes exist, litigation is pending, and daily life inside the division is protected by operative, ballot-confirmed law. Border exposure is narrower, though documented federal custody abuse is worse than Vellandra's non-custodial harm.

Kestrel Isles offers discretionary secondary screening, administrative refusal, slow appeal and no criminal route. Our entry exposure is worse: policy-directed refusal plus possible lifetime fraud ineligibility, and far worse custody outcomes if detention follows. But the division's documented protections — public accommodations, hate-crime reporting, shield law, self-ID documents — substantially exceed Kestrel's protections. Net placement is similar, pulled slightly down by the custody record.

Meridia trains border officers, accepts matching markers, and guarantees counsel and compensation for brief detention. Our federal regime reverses each element: marker restrictions upheld, refusal directed by cable, and trans detainees documented as beaten and sexually abused. Stronger in-state protections than Meridia's do not offset a hostile entry and custody layer, so this rating sits materially below 0.75-C.

Luskaine's officer demanded sex disclosure while regulation prohibited it, and a border advocate secured approval — hostile frontline, protective rule. Here the rule itself is hostile (executive order plus cable directing refusal), making exposure more systematic, yet the division supplies protections (shield law, accommodations, hate-crime machinery) Luskaine lacks. Mixed against mixed, this rating sits a little below 0.65-E.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller meets one system with two layers. Inside the division, the documented protections actually operate: public accommodations retained by popular vote, gender-identity hate-crime coverage with mandatory public reporting, self-ID documents, confidential name changes and a shield law that follows the visitor's own care needs. Outing in hotels, shops or restaurants there yields friction with real recourse, not danger. The federal layer, however, governs the stages no state law reaches — visa adjudication, border inspection, federally funded facilities and immigration custody — and is documented as hostile: refusal directed at document discrepancy, marker restrictions upheld by the Supreme Court, and a pattern of identity-motivated abuse in detention. The chain discrepancy → investigation → federal custody is the operative worst case, so protective local law lifts this above the national line but cannot carry it into Low Risk while that federal exposure is unremedied and partly litigated.
